title: What is a Distributed System?
explanation: A distributed system is a collection of independent computers that appear to users as a single coherent system. They work together over a network to achieve common goals, sharing the workload and providing redundancy.
analogy: Like a restaurant with multiple kitchens in different locations. Customers order from one menu, unaware that their food might come from the nearest kitchen.
example: Google Search runs on thousands of computers worldwide. When you search, your request hits nearby servers that coordinate to return results in milliseconds.
why_it_matters: Modern applications must handle millions of users and petabytes of data. No single computer is powerful enough - distribution is the only way.
checkpoint_question: Why can't we just use one really powerful computer instead of distributing across many?
expected_answer: Physical limits (one CPU can only be so fast), reliability (single point of failure), cost (distributed commodity hardware is cheaper than supercomputers), geography (users need servers nearby for low latency).
common_mistake: Thinking distributed systems are always better. They add complexity. Use them when you actually need scale or redundancy.
key_insight: The fallacies of distributed computing: network is reliable, latency is zero, bandwidth is infinite, network is secure, topology doesn't change. All are false.

title: Why Distributed Systems are Hard
explanation: Distributed systems face unique challenges: network can fail or delay messages, clocks aren't perfectly synchronized, components fail independently, and concurrent updates can conflict. These don't exist in single-computer programs.
analogy: Like coordinating a group project when everyone is in different time zones, has unreliable phones, and might go silent at any moment.
example: Node A sends 'set value=10' to Node B, then 'set value=20' to Node C. Due to network delays, C processes first. Now B has 20, C has 10. Which is correct?
why_it_matters: Distributed system bugs are subtle and hard to reproduce. Understanding the fundamental challenges helps you design correct systems.
checkpoint_question: What can go wrong when sending a message from Server A to Server B?
expected_answer: Message could be lost, delayed arbitrarily, duplicated, delivered out of order, or corrupted. A might not know if B received it. B might receive it but A's acknowledgment might be lost. A and B can't distinguish slow from dead.
common_mistake: Assuming the network always works. Design for failure from the start - it's not optional.
key_insight: Two Generals Problem: you can't guarantee two parties agree on something using only unreliable communication. This is fundamental.

title: The CAP Theorem
explanation: CAP states that during a network partition, a distributed system must choose between Consistency (all nodes see the same data) and Availability (every request gets a response). You can't have both when the network fails.
analogy: Two bank branches lose phone connection. They can either stop all transactions (consistent but unavailable) or let branches operate independently (available but inconsistent until reconnected).
example: During partition: CP system (MongoDB with majority reads) rejects requests if it can't reach majority. AP system (Cassandra) allows writes but nodes may have different values.
why_it_matters: CAP forces you to make explicit tradeoffs. Understanding it helps you choose the right database and design for your use case.
checkpoint_question: Why can't a distributed database be both consistent and available during a network partition?
expected_answer: If nodes can't communicate, they face a choice: reject operations (consistent but unavailable) or accept them independently (available but potentially inconsistent). Without communication, they can't guarantee they agree.
common_mistake: Thinking you must choose one of C, A, P. During normal operation you get all three. CAP only forces a choice during partitions.
key_insight: PACELC extends CAP: during Partition, choose A or C; Else (normal operation), choose Latency or Consistency.

title: Consistency Models
explanation: Consistency models define what values a read can return. Strong consistency: always see the latest write. Eventual consistency: updates propagate eventually, may see stale data temporarily. Weaker models allow more flexibility but require careful programming.
analogy: Strong: everyone in a meeting hears the same thing simultaneously. Eventual: news spreading - not everyone knows immediately, but eventually all do.
example: Strong: Bank balance always reflects all transactions. Eventual: Instagram likes - you might see 99 likes while another user sees 101. Both converge to 100 eventually.
why_it_matters: Consistency is often the first thing sacrificed for performance. Understanding the tradeoffs lets you make informed architectural decisions.
checkpoint_question: When is eventual consistency acceptable?
expected_answer: When temporary inconsistency doesn't cause harm: social media likes, view counts, shopping cart, user sessions. Not acceptable for: financial transactions, inventory counts going negative, security permissions.
common_mistake: Assuming strong consistency is always required. It's expensive. Many applications work fine with eventual consistency.
key_insight: Between strong and eventual are models like causal consistency (cause precedes effect) and read-your-writes (you see your own updates).

title: Consensus Algorithms
explanation: Consensus algorithms help distributed nodes agree on a value even when some nodes fail or messages are lost. They're the foundation of reliable distributed systems. Popular ones: Paxos, Raft, Zab.
analogy: Like getting a group to decide on a restaurant when some members aren't responding to texts. You need a protocol that works despite partial communication.
example: Raft elects a leader. Clients send updates to the leader. Leader replicates to followers. Once a majority confirms, the update is committed. If leader fails, a new one is elected.
why_it_matters: Consensus is how databases replicate data reliably. Understanding it helps you reason about what guarantees your systems provide.
checkpoint_question: Why do consensus algorithms require a majority of nodes?
expected_answer: Any two majorities overlap by at least one node. This guarantees the committed value is known. With 5 nodes, any majority (3+) overlaps. If only 2 of 5 agree, a different 2 might agree on something else.
common_mistake: Implementing your own consensus. It's notoriously difficult. Use proven implementations like etcd (Raft) or ZooKeeper (Zab).
key_insight: Consensus requires at least 3 nodes to tolerate 1 failure, 5 to tolerate 2. Formula: 2f+1 nodes to tolerate f failures.

title: Data Replication
explanation: Replication copies data to multiple nodes for redundancy and performance. If one node fails, others have the data. Reads can be served from any replica. The challenge is keeping replicas synchronized.
analogy: Like having backup copies of important documents in multiple safes. Lose one safe, you still have the data. But when you update, you must update all copies.
example: MySQL primary-replica replication: writes go to primary, which sends changes to replicas. Replicas serve reads. If primary fails, promote a replica to primary.
why_it_matters: Replication is fundamental to reliability and performance. Understanding replication strategies helps you design resilient data architectures.
checkpoint_question: What's the tradeoff between synchronous and asynchronous replication?
expected_answer: Synchronous: write confirmed only after all replicas acknowledge. No data loss but higher latency, blocks on slow replicas. Asynchronous: write confirmed immediately, replicated later. Lower latency but can lose recent writes if primary fails.
common_mistake: Assuming replicas are instantly updated. Replication lag means replicas might be seconds or minutes behind.
key_insight: Multi-leader replication allows writes to multiple nodes (good for geo-distribution) but requires conflict resolution.

title: Quorum Reads and Writes
explanation: In a quorum system, you write to W nodes and read from R nodes. If W + R > N (total nodes), at least one node you read from has the latest write. This provides tunable consistency without requiring all nodes.
analogy: If 3 people each have a piece of news, and you ask 2 people, you're guaranteed to find someone with the latest. The overlap ensures you don't miss updates.
example: N=3, W=2, R=2. Write to 2 nodes. Read from 2 nodes. W+R=4 > 3, so reads always see latest write. If you want faster reads, use R=1 but W=3 (write to all).
why_it_matters: Quorums let you balance consistency, availability, and latency. It's a fundamental technique in distributed databases.
checkpoint_question: With N=5 nodes, what values of W and R guarantee you always read the latest write?
expected_answer: W + R > 5, so W + R >= 6. Examples: W=3, R=3 or W=4, R=2 or W=2, R=4. Higher W means slower writes but faster reads. Higher R means faster writes but slower reads.
common_mistake: Forgetting about failures. If 2 of 5 nodes are down and you need W=3, writes fail. Consider failure scenarios in your quorum design.
key_insight: DynamoDB, Cassandra, and Riak all use quorum-based systems with tunable consistency.

title: Data Partitioning (Sharding)
explanation: Partitioning splits data across multiple nodes, each holding a subset. This enables horizontal scaling - add more nodes to handle more data. The partition key determines which node holds each record.
analogy: Like organizing a library across multiple buildings by author's last name. A-M in Building 1, N-Z in Building 2. To find a book, you know which building to check.
example: Shard users by user_id % 4. User 12 goes to shard 0, user 15 to shard 3. Each shard holds ~25% of users. Add more shards to scale further.
why_it_matters: Partitioning is how databases scale beyond a single machine. Understanding it helps you design for growth.
checkpoint_question: What makes a good partition key?
expected_answer: High cardinality (many unique values), even distribution (no hot spots), matches access patterns (queries mostly access one partition). Bad: boolean values, time-based keys that create hot recent partition.
common_mistake: Choosing a partition key that creates hot spots. One shard getting all the traffic defeats the purpose.
key_insight: Cross-partition queries are expensive. Design your data model so most queries hit a single partition.

title: Consistent Hashing
explanation: Consistent hashing distributes data across nodes so adding/removing nodes only moves a small fraction of data. Nodes and keys are placed on a hash ring. Each key is stored on the next node clockwise.
analogy: Like seats around a circular table. Adding a person only affects their neighbors. Others keep their seats.
example: Hash ring 0-360. Nodes at positions 90, 180, 270. Key hashes to 100 -> goes to node at 180. Add node at 135 -> only keys 91-135 move to new node, rest unchanged.
why_it_matters: Consistent hashing minimizes data movement during scaling. It's used in caches (Memcached), databases (Cassandra), and CDNs.
checkpoint_question: Why is consistent hashing better than simple modulo hashing (key % num_nodes)?
expected_answer: With modulo, adding a node changes nearly all key assignments. With consistent hashing, only keys between the new node and its predecessor move. This dramatically reduces data movement during scaling.
common_mistake: Not using virtual nodes. With few physical nodes, distribution can be uneven. Virtual nodes give each physical node multiple positions on the ring.
key_insight: Virtual nodes: each physical node gets many positions on the ring, ensuring more even distribution.

title: Logical Clocks
explanation: Physical clocks in distributed systems can't be perfectly synchronized. Logical clocks capture the order of events without needing synchronized time. Lamport timestamps and vector clocks are common approaches.
analogy: Like sequence numbers on bank checks. You can tell check 102 came after 101 without knowing the exact time each was written.
example: Node A sends message with timestamp 5 to Node B. B increments to 6 and responds. A receives, increments to 7. The timestamps capture causal ordering.
why_it_matters: Understanding logical time is essential for reasoning about concurrent events in distributed systems.
checkpoint_question: Why can't we rely on physical timestamps to order events in a distributed system?
expected_answer: Clocks drift and can't be perfectly synchronized. Events might have identical timestamps. Clock skew can make B's event appear before A's even if A caused B. NTP synchronization is only approximate.
common_mistake: Using timestamps to order events in different systems. Wall clock time is unreliable across machines.
code:
# Lamport Timestamp
class LamportClock:
    def __init__(self):
        self.time = 0
    
    def tick(self):  # Local event
        self.time += 1
        return self.time
    
    def receive(self, msg_time):  # On message receipt
        self.time = max(self.time, msg_time) + 1
        return self.time
key_insight: Lamport timestamps show 'happened-before' relationship. Vector clocks can detect concurrent events.

title: Vector Clocks
explanation: Vector clocks extend Lamport timestamps. Each node maintains a vector of timestamps, one per node. This lets you detect both causality and concurrency - two events that neither caused the other.
analogy: Like each person tracking their count plus counts from everyone they've communicated with. Comparing vectors shows who has seen what.
example: Node A: [A=2, B=1]. Node B: [A=1, B=3]. Neither dominates the other (2>1 but 1<3), so their latest events are concurrent - happened independently.
why_it_matters: Vector clocks enable conflict detection in eventually consistent systems. You can tell when two writes happened independently and need resolution.
checkpoint_question: How do you know if event X happened before event Y using vector clocks?
expected_answer: X happened-before Y if X's vector is less than or equal to Y's vector in all components, and strictly less in at least one. If neither is true in either direction, X and Y are concurrent.
common_mistake: Confusing concurrent with simultaneous. Concurrent means neither caused the other - they could happen at very different times but with no communication between.
key_insight: Vector clocks grow with number of nodes. For large systems, dotted version vectors or interval tree clocks are more space-efficient.

title: Failure Detection
explanation: Detecting failures is hard because you can't distinguish a dead node from a slow one or a network partition. Heartbeat protocols detect failures probabilistically - if a node misses several heartbeats, assume it's dead.
analogy: Like check-in texts with friends. If someone doesn't respond for a day, they might be busy or their phone might be broken. You can't be certain.
example: Nodes send heartbeats every 1 second. Miss 3 heartbeats = suspected dead. But the 'dead' node might just be slow or network-partitioned. It might still be running and serving requests.
why_it_matters: Incorrect failure detection causes problems: false positives trigger unnecessary failovers, false negatives leave dead nodes in rotation.
checkpoint_question: What's the danger of incorrectly detecting a node as dead?
expected_answer: Split-brain: the 'dead' node is actually alive. Now two nodes think they're the leader, accepting conflicting writes. When they reconnect, data is inconsistent. Clients may get different answers from different nodes.
common_mistake: Setting heartbeat timeouts too aggressive. Network hiccups cause false positives. Too conservative and real failures aren't detected quickly.
key_insight: Phi Accrual failure detector adjusts suspicion levels based on historical heartbeat timing rather than fixed timeouts.

title: Byzantine Fault Tolerance
explanation: Byzantine faults occur when nodes malfunction arbitrarily - sending wrong data, lying about state, or acting maliciously. BFT algorithms handle these, but require 3f+1 nodes to tolerate f Byzantine failures.
analogy: Regular failures: soldier doesn't respond (dead). Byzantine: soldier lies about enemy position. Handling lies is much harder than handling silence.
example: In Bitcoin, Byzantine nodes might try to spend the same coin twice. The blockchain uses proof-of-work as a BFT mechanism - the longest chain wins.
why_it_matters: Most systems assume crash-only failures. If you need security against malicious actors (blockchain, military systems), you need BFT.
checkpoint_question: Why do Byzantine fault tolerant systems need more nodes than crash fault tolerant ones?
expected_answer: With crashes, silent nodes are clearly dead. With Byzantine faults, malicious nodes might lie. To out-vote f liars, you need 2f+1 honest nodes. Total: 3f+1. Crash tolerance only needs 2f+1 total.
common_mistake: Using BFT when you don't need it. BFT is expensive (more nodes, more communication). Use it only when you don't trust participants.
key_insight: Practical BFT (PBFT) works for small node counts. For large scale, blockchain-style consensus uses economics (proof-of-stake) rather than pure algorithm.

title: Distributed Transactions
explanation: A distributed transaction spans multiple nodes or services. All must commit or all must abort - partial success is not allowed. This requires coordination protocols like two-phase commit.
analogy: Like multiple departments signing off on a contract. All must agree before it's official. One rejection cancels the whole thing.
example: Transfer $100 from Account A (Bank 1) to Account B (Bank 2). Must debit A and credit B atomically. If either fails, both operations must be undone.
why_it_matters: Distributed transactions maintain consistency across services. Understanding their costs helps you design around them when possible.
checkpoint_question: Why are distributed transactions slower than local transactions?
expected_answer: Network round-trips for coordination. Two-phase commit requires prepare, acknowledge, commit messages. Locks held during coordination block other transactions. Any participant failure stalls the transaction.
common_mistake: Overusing distributed transactions. They're expensive. Often you can redesign to keep transactions local or use eventual consistency.
key_insight: Sagas break transactions into steps with compensating actions. If step 3 fails, run compensations for steps 1 and 2. More available but eventually consistent.

title: Two-Phase Commit
explanation: 2PC is a protocol for atomic commits across multiple nodes. Phase 1: coordinator asks all participants if they can commit (prepare). Phase 2: if all say yes, coordinator tells all to commit; if any says no, all abort.
analogy: Like a wedding. Officiant asks 'Do you?' to each person. Only if both say yes does the marriage happen. One 'no' cancels everything.
example: Coordinator: 'Prepare to commit txn123?' Node A: 'Yes, prepared.' Node B: 'Yes, prepared.' Coordinator: 'Commit txn123.' Both nodes commit. Transaction complete.
why_it_matters: 2PC is the classic solution to distributed transactions. Understanding its flaws explains why alternatives exist.
checkpoint_question: What happens if the coordinator crashes after sending 'prepare' but before sending 'commit'?
expected_answer: Participants are stuck - they've promised to commit but don't know if they should. They're holding locks, blocking other transactions. Must wait for coordinator recovery. This is 2PC's blocking problem.
common_mistake: Using 2PC across unreliable networks. A partitioned coordinator blocks all participants indefinitely.
key_insight: 3PC (Three-Phase Commit) adds a pre-commit phase to reduce blocking, but still has edge cases. Consensus-based commits are more robust.

title: Saga Pattern
explanation: Sagas break a distributed transaction into local transactions with compensating actions. If any step fails, execute compensations in reverse order. Unlike 2PC, sagas don't hold locks - they're eventually consistent.
analogy: Like planning a vacation: book flight, book hotel, book car. If car rental fails, don't hold the reservations - cancel hotel, cancel flight.
example: Order saga: 1) Reserve inventory, 2) Charge payment, 3) Ship order. If shipping fails: compensate by refunding payment, then unreserving inventory.
why_it_matters: Sagas enable long-running transactions without blocking. They're the preferred pattern for microservices.
checkpoint_question: How do sagas handle a failure during compensation?
expected_answer: Compensations must be idempotent (safe to retry) and eventually succeed. If a compensation keeps failing, you need manual intervention or dead letter queues. Design compensations carefully.
common_mistake: Not making compensations idempotent. If compensation is retried (after timeout), duplicate execution must be safe.
key_insight: Choreography sagas: services react to events. Orchestration sagas: central coordinator directs steps. Each has tradeoffs.

title: Message Queues
explanation: Message queues decouple senders from receivers. Senders put messages on the queue; receivers process them when ready. If a receiver is slow or down, messages wait in the queue rather than being lost.
analogy: Like a mail drop-off. You don't wait for the recipient to be home. Drop the letter; they'll pick it up later.
example: Web server puts 'send welcome email' message in queue. Email worker processes the queue at its own pace. Web server responds immediately without waiting for email to send.
why_it_matters: Queues enable asynchronous processing, improve reliability, and handle traffic spikes by buffering work.
checkpoint_question: What's the difference between a message queue and direct API calls?
expected_answer: API calls are synchronous - sender waits. Queues are async - sender continues immediately. Queues buffer work, so receiver downtime doesn't fail senders. Queues enable retry and rate limiting naturally.
common_mistake: Not handling duplicate messages. Most queues guarantee at-least-once delivery, not exactly-once. Make consumers idempotent.
key_insight: Point-to-point queues (SQS): one consumer gets each message. Pub/sub (SNS, Kafka): all subscribers get each message.

title: Exactly-Once Semantics
explanation: Message delivery has three guarantees: at-most-once (may lose messages), at-least-once (may duplicate), exactly-once (each message processed once). True exactly-once is impossible; it's achieved through idempotency.
analogy: Sending a letter: regular mail might lose it. Certified mail might send duplicates if receipt is lost. 'Exactly-once' means the recipient ignores duplicates.
example: Payment system: at-least-once delivery might charge a customer twice. To achieve effectively-exactly-once, include transaction ID and ignore duplicates in the processor.
why_it_matters: Understanding delivery semantics helps you design systems that behave correctly despite duplicates or losses.
checkpoint_question: How do you achieve effectively-exactly-once processing with at-least-once delivery?
expected_answer: Make message processing idempotent. Track processed message IDs and skip duplicates. Use database transactions: read message, process, mark complete atomically. Retry failures safely.
common_mistake: Assuming the messaging system handles exactly-once. Most don't. The consumer must be designed for it.
code:
# Idempotent message processing
def process_payment(message):
    txn_id = message['transaction_id']
    
    # Check if already processed
    if db.exists(f'processed:{txn_id}'):
        return  # Skip duplicate
    
    # Process payment
    charge_card(message['amount'])
    
    # Mark as processed
    db.set(f'processed:{txn_id}', True)
key_insight: Kafka achieves exactly-once within its ecosystem by combining idempotent producers and transactional consumers.

title: Event Sourcing
explanation: Event sourcing stores all changes as a sequence of events rather than current state. To get current state, replay all events. This provides a complete audit log and enables rebuilding state at any point in time.
analogy: Like a bank statement vs. balance. The balance is current state; the statement (events) shows how you got there and lets you verify or reconstruct.
example: Order events: OrderCreated, ItemAdded, ItemRemoved, OrderSubmitted, OrderShipped. Current order state is derived by replaying these events. You can answer 'what was the order before shipping?'
why_it_matters: Event sourcing enables audit logs, temporal queries, and easy debugging. It's powerful for financial systems and complex domains.
checkpoint_question: How do you handle millions of events when reconstructing current state?
expected_answer: Use snapshots. Periodically save current state as a checkpoint. To rebuild, load latest snapshot then replay only events after it. Balance between snapshot frequency and replay overhead.
common_mistake: Using event sourcing everywhere. It adds complexity. Use it when you need audit trails or temporal queries, not for simple CRUD.
key_insight: CQRS (Command Query Responsibility Segregation) often pairs with event sourcing: events update write model, read models are optimized projections.

title: Distributed Caching
explanation: A distributed cache spreads cached data across multiple nodes. This scales beyond single-machine memory and survives individual node failures. Popular implementations: Redis Cluster, Memcached.
analogy: Like having multiple refrigerators in different parts of a large kitchen. Food is distributed so chefs can grab ingredients quickly from nearby fridges.
example: Redis Cluster with 6 nodes: data is partitioned across nodes using hash slots. Key 'user:123' might live on node 3. Clients route requests to the right node.
why_it_matters: Caching is critical for performance. Understanding distributed caching helps you scale beyond single-node limits.
checkpoint_question: What happens when a node in a distributed cache fails?
expected_answer: That node's data is temporarily unavailable (cache miss). With replication, replicas serve the data. Without replication, requests fall through to the database. The cluster rebalances to handle the missing node.
common_mistake: Not handling cache misses gracefully. Your system must work without the cache - just slower. Never let cache failures cause outages.
key_insight: Cache-aside: app checks cache, on miss reads DB and populates cache. Write-through: writes go to cache, cache writes to DB.

title: Cache Invalidation
explanation: When data changes, cached copies become stale. Cache invalidation ensures caches reflect current data. This is famously hard - Phil Karlton said: 'There are only two hard things: cache invalidation and naming things.'
analogy: Like recalling newspapers after printing a mistake. You published copies everywhere - how do you ensure everyone sees the correction?
example: User updates profile. Cache has old data. Options: 1) Delete cache key (next read refills), 2) Update cache directly, 3) Set TTL and accept staleness temporarily.
why_it_matters: Stale caches cause bugs and user confusion. Understanding invalidation strategies helps you maintain consistency.
checkpoint_question: Why might you prefer TTL-based expiration over explicit invalidation?
expected_answer: TTL is simpler - no need to track what's cached where. It's eventually consistent (data updates within TTL). Explicit invalidation requires knowing all cache keys affected by a change, which can be complex.
common_mistake: Using long TTLs and explicit invalidation but forgetting edge cases. Some data changes don't trigger invalidation, leaving stale data.
key_insight: Write-through caches update cache on write, avoiding staleness. But cache and DB updates must be atomic - tricky in distributed systems.

title: Circuit Breaker Pattern
explanation: A circuit breaker prevents cascading failures. When a service fails repeatedly, the breaker 'opens' - calls fail fast without trying the service. After a timeout, it allows test requests to check if the service recovered.
analogy: Like an electrical circuit breaker. When there's a surge, it trips to prevent damage. You reset it once the problem is fixed.
example: Payment service is down. Without circuit breaker: every checkout tries payment, waits for timeout, makes users wait 30s. With circuit breaker: after 5 failures, calls fail instantly. Users see 'try again later' immediately.
why_it_matters: Circuit breakers prevent a failing service from taking down the entire system. They're essential for resilient microservices.
checkpoint_question: What are the three states of a circuit breaker?
expected_answer: Closed: requests flow normally. Open: requests fail immediately without calling the service. Half-open: allow a few test requests; if they succeed, close the breaker; if they fail, reopen.
common_mistake: Not handling open circuit gracefully. Return degraded functionality or cached data, not just errors.
key_insight: Libraries like Hystrix (deprecated), Resilience4j, and Polly implement circuit breakers. Don't implement from scratch.

title: Bulkhead Pattern
explanation: The bulkhead pattern isolates failures by partitioning resources. Like compartments in a ship, a breach in one doesn't sink the whole ship. If one dependency fails, only its partition is affected.
analogy: Like a ship with sealed compartments. If one floods, others stay dry. The ship stays afloat.
example: Web server has two thread pools: 100 threads for product API, 50 for payment API. If payment gets slow and consumes all its threads, product API still works with its separate pool.
why_it_matters: Bulkheads prevent a slow or failing dependency from consuming all resources and causing total system failure.
checkpoint_question: How does a bulkhead differ from a circuit breaker?
expected_answer: Circuit breaker stops calling a failing service. Bulkhead limits resources per service even when healthy. They're complementary: bulkhead prevents resource exhaustion, circuit breaker prevents wasted calls to dead services.
common_mistake: Setting bulkhead limits too high. If each of 5 services can use 100 threads and you only have 200 threads total, bulkheads overlap and don't isolate.
key_insight: Kubernetes resource limits are a form of bulkhead - preventing one pod from consuming all cluster resources.

title: Retry with Backoff
explanation: When a request fails, retry it - but with increasing delays (exponential backoff) and randomization (jitter). This gives the failing service time to recover without overwhelming it with retry storms.
analogy: Like trying to call someone who's busy. You don't redial immediately 100 times. Wait 1 minute, then 5, then 15. Maybe they're in a meeting.
example: First retry after 1s, second after 2s, third after 4s, fourth after 8s. Add random jitter (0-1s) so retries don't all happen simultaneously.
why_it_matters: Without backoff, retries can worsen outages. Thousands of clients retrying immediately create a thundering herd that prevents recovery.
checkpoint_question: Why add random jitter to retry delays?
expected_answer: Without jitter, all clients retry at the same intervals, creating synchronized traffic spikes. Jitter spreads retries randomly over time, smoothing the load on the recovering service.
common_mistake: Retrying non-idempotent operations. If you're not sure the request failed (timeout), retry might cause duplicates. Only retry idempotent operations safely.
key_insight: Set a maximum retry count and total timeout. Infinite retries with backoff still retry forever.

title: Stream Processing
explanation: Stream processing handles continuous data flows in real-time rather than batch processing stored data. Events are processed as they arrive, enabling immediate reactions to changes.
analogy: Batch processing: reading all emails at end of day. Stream processing: handling each email as it arrives throughout the day.
example: Real-time fraud detection: each transaction is analyzed as it happens. Stream processor checks patterns, blocks suspicious transactions instantly rather than in overnight batch.
why_it_matters: Many applications need real-time responses: fraud detection, monitoring, live dashboards, recommendations. Batch processing is too slow.
checkpoint_question: What's the tradeoff between stream processing and batch processing?
expected_answer: Stream: low latency but processes events individually (less efficient, harder to get global view). Batch: higher latency but can optimize across entire dataset (more efficient, complete picture).
common_mistake: Processing events without handling late-arriving data. Network delays mean events arrive out of order. Account for this in your processing logic.
key_insight: Lambda architecture combines batch (accuracy) and stream (speed). Kappa architecture uses streams for everything with replay capability.

title: CRDTs: Conflict-Free Replicated Data Types
explanation: CRDTs are data structures that can be replicated across nodes and updated independently. All replicas automatically converge to the same state without coordination. They enable offline-capable apps and geo-distributed systems.
analogy: Like Google Docs collaboration. Multiple people edit simultaneously without explicit coordination. The document converges to include everyone's changes.
example: G-Counter CRDT: each node keeps its own count. To merge, take max of each node's count. [A:5, B:3] + [A:4, B:6] = [A:5, B:6]. Total: 11. Always converges.
why_it_matters: CRDTs enable eventual consistency without complex conflict resolution. They're the technology behind collaborative editing and distributed databases.
checkpoint_question: Why do CRDTs converge without coordination?
expected_answer: CRDT operations are designed to be commutative, associative, and idempotent. Order doesn't matter. Applying same update twice has no extra effect. Any merge order produces the same result.
common_mistake: Thinking CRDTs solve all conflict problems. They work for specific data types. General-purpose conflict resolution still needs application logic.
key_insight: LWW-Register (Last-Writer-Wins) uses timestamps. PN-Counter supports decrement (two G-Counters). OR-Set (Observed-Remove) handles set operations.

title: Service Discovery
explanation: In dynamic environments, services move around - IPs change, instances scale up/down. Service discovery tracks which instances are available and routes requests to healthy ones.
analogy: Like a phone directory that updates in real-time. You look up 'Payment Service' and get current phone numbers for available employees.
example: Order service needs Payment service. Asks Consul: 'Where is payment?' Gets IPs of 3 healthy instances. Consul removes unhealthy instances automatically.
why_it_matters: Hard-coded IPs break when services move. Service discovery is essential for dynamic, auto-scaling systems.
checkpoint_question: How does a service register itself with a service discovery system?
expected_answer: Self-registration: service starts, calls discovery API to register with its IP/port, sends heartbeats. Third-party: deployment system registers services. Deregistration on shutdown or after missed heartbeats.
common_mistake: Not handling stale registrations. If a service crashes without deregistering, discovery returns dead instances. Use health checks.
key_insight: Client-side discovery: client queries registry, chooses instance. Server-side discovery: load balancer queries registry, routes requests.

title: Chaos Engineering
explanation: Chaos engineering proactively tests system resilience by injecting failures: killing instances, introducing latency, simulating network partitions. It finds weaknesses before real incidents do.
analogy: Like a fire drill. You cause a controlled 'fire' to see if evacuation procedures work, rather than discovering problems during a real fire.
example: Netflix Chaos Monkey randomly kills production instances. If the system isn't resilient, the failure exposes it. Teams fix weaknesses before they cause real outages.
why_it_matters: Distributed systems fail in unexpected ways. Chaos engineering builds confidence that your resilience measures actually work.
checkpoint_question: Why run chaos experiments in production rather than just in testing environments?
expected_answer: Testing environments don't mirror production exactly: different traffic patterns, data volumes, configurations. Production chaos finds real issues. Start small (single instance, off-peak hours) and expand.
common_mistake: Running chaos without a hypothesis. Define what you expect to happen. Compare with actual results. Random failure injection without analysis isn't useful.
key_insight: The Principles of Chaos Engineering: define steady state, hypothesize, introduce variables, try to disprove hypothesis.

title: Distributed Systems Testing
explanation: Testing distributed systems is uniquely hard. Bugs emerge from timing, ordering, and partial failures that are difficult to reproduce. Special techniques: deterministic simulation, property-based testing, and formal verification.
analogy: Like testing a recipe that varies based on kitchen temperature, humidity, and ingredient suppliers. You can't just test once - you need to test many scenarios.
example: FoundationDB uses deterministic simulation: the entire distributed database runs in a single thread with controlled time and network. They test years of simulated operation with injected failures.
why_it_matters: Normal unit tests don't catch distributed system bugs. Special testing strategies are required for confidence in correctness.
checkpoint_question: Why are distributed system bugs hard to reproduce?
expected_answer: They depend on timing, network delays, and ordering of concurrent events. Re-running the same test produces different interleavings. The bug might require specific rare conditions that don't occur in normal testing.
common_mistake: Thinking 'it passed tests' means it's correct. Distributed bugs hide. Use formal methods, property testing, and chaos engineering.
key_insight: Jepsen tests distributed databases by injecting partitions and checking for data loss or inconsistency. Many databases have failed Jepsen tests.

title: Designing for Failure
explanation: In distributed systems, failure is not exceptional - it's expected. Design with the assumption that any component can fail at any time. Embrace redundancy, graceful degradation, and explicit failure handling.
analogy: Like designing buildings in earthquake zones. You don't hope earthquakes won't happen - you engineer the building to survive them.
example: Netflix: if recommendations service fails, show popular content instead. If payments fail, queue the charge for retry. Nothing is designed to be critical enough to cause total outage.
why_it_matters: Users don't care why something failed. Building resilient systems means they experience minimal disruption despite constant background failures.
checkpoint_question: What does 'graceful degradation' mean in practice?
expected_answer: When a component fails, provide reduced but functional service instead of total failure. Examples: show cached data instead of live data, disable non-essential features, queue requests for later processing.
common_mistake: Designing the happy path first, adding error handling later. Design for failure from the start - it's not an afterthought.
key_insight: Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) uses error budgets: allow a percentage of failures. If under budget, ship faster. If over, focus on reliability.
